newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Privatisation key to Yugo finance market - experts.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation key to Yugo finance market - experts.

text.p: The slow pace of privatisation in Yugoslavia is blocking the development of financial markets crucial for the country's move to a market economy, financial analysts said on Wednesday.

At a symposium of some 400 Yugoslav financial and economic experts at this Montenegran seaside resort, one participant said rump Yugoslavia was "five or six steps" behind some other East European countries in developing financial markets.

"We are now in the first class of elementary school and the other east European countries are already finishing it -- that is how we stand on financial markets," the expert, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
Yugoslavia, now made up of Serbia and Montenegro, was hit by U.N. trade sanctions imposed in May, 1992, for its role in the Bosnian war, and these were lifted only last November.
An "outer ring" of sanctions still exists barring Belgrade from access to international financial institutions, but is expected to be lifted shortly.

Veselin Vukotic, president of the association of Montenegran economists, told Reuters the financial market was the heart of an open market economy, adding: "We have to realise its importance as we have opted for a free and open market."
According to Vukotic, privatisation is the key to the development of Yugoslavia's financial markets.

"Activities on the financial markets will not pick up without transparent and relatively quick privatisation," he said. "We have to break the illusion that any significant inflow of foreign funds will happen before we have a well-prepared infrastructure and good investment projects."
Many analysts doubted whether there would be any quick progress on privatisation, because of problems in clarifying ownership and improving the legal environment for business and finance.
There was also opposition to privatisation from company managers, analysts said.
"It cannot be left to the managers to decide whether to privatise the company or not as it is envisaged by the current federal law," one banker said. "Privatisation has to be obligatory".
Experts say the legal framework of the country's financial market is more or less satisfactory -- a regulatory body, two official bourses, 18 licensed brokerages and one rating agency already exist.
"Yugoslavia is in a much better position today than it was yesterday," Pava Zecevic, the director of the Belgrade Stock Exchange said.

She said the suspension of sanctions had opened up new possibilities to develop domestic financial markets. "We have to adjust our regulations with the existing rules on world markets, which we could not have done under the embargo."
Yugoslavia's securities agency has granted around $3.6 billion worth of shares in the past six years, but many companies decline to list their shares on the official market.
There is no secondary market despite the existence of a good base, Stojan Dabic, a prominent financial expert said. "We must define and remove current obstacles," he said.
